Sourcing enough electricity for data centres

Global electricity consumption by data centres nearly doubled in five years between 2020 and 2025, and is expected to almost double again by 2030, which will require large amounts of additional generation. 

Data centres accounted for just 1.5% of global electricity consumption in 2025 and the share is forecast to remain well below 5% through 2030 under all scenarios modelled by the International Energy Agency (IEA).  

But data centres are strongly clustered in a small number of countries, and within them a small number of regions, a pattern that is expected to persist in the medium term. 

Most of the forecast growth in data centres over the next five years is set to occur within existing clusters, which will intensify pressure on electricity networks.

The IEA estimates more than half of the new data centres under construction or already announced but not yet at the building stage are located within existing clusters.

Data centres are imposing only a modest additional load on electricity system at global scale but the impact is much more concentrated and severe in local areas ...

U.S. REFINERS processed an average of 17.4 million barrels per day of crude and other feedstocks over the seven days ending on September 11. Processing was almost 0.5 million b/d higher than at the same point in 2025 and 2024 as refiners captured near-record margins and sought to offset the global shortage of gasoline and especially diesel. Processing was the fastest for the time of year since before the pandemic in 2019, despite a reduction in capacity, which resulted in exceptionally high rates of utilisation above 96%:

The reason the endgame scenario started to form for me wasn’t because of JPM’s piece about how they can’t model the endgame. It was because of this vitally important news today about the Saudis pleading with China to help get the oil out of the Oman lane.

From the start of this conflict, China has been the black-box variable, but some of its recent actions make me think I may have read China’s incentives correctly from the start.

For China, the Strait of Hormuz issue is also an all-or-nothing dilemma. If the US were to win the war and restore the Strait to its pre-war status, the security arrangements that would need to be put in place to prevent another closure by Iran would almost guarantee that China would be held hostage at a later date.

Conversely, if Iran controls the Strait, China would effectively become the region’s new peace guarantor. Geopolitically, this is the move of the century.

Gold’s post-FOMC rate-hike recovery suggests the move was fully priced, while Warsh’s attempt to stabilise the bond market - arguably a key reason for hiking - has so far been relatively successful, helped by the sharp pullback in oil prices and the resulting easing of inflation concerns.

It is also impressive to see gold ETF holdings climb to a seven-month high, despite the recent price wobble, highlighting a market where demand from less interest-rate-sensitive investors remains firm despite elevated yields.

Next up is the resistance area mentioned in my earlier post, which should help determine whether this recovery has further room to run. Back from travelling on Monday, when I will take a closer look.
